newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam denies coffee quality problems.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam denies coffee quality problems.

text.p: Vietnam's state coffee corporation, Vinacafe, lashed out on Monday at reports that beans from the country's main producing area were being hit by mould problems and said producers were being urged to focus on quality.

Doan Trieu Nhan, Vinacafe's vice-president, told a briefing in Hanoi for traders and journalists that a foreign news report last week which said Vietnamese beans from Daklak were suffering high mould levels was incorrect.
"If a report says the quality is unacceptable, it's wrong," he said. "A 0.1 to 0.2 percent mould rate is normal, but the report said the percentage was was from 3-4 percent."
Nhan also dismissed local press reports that farmers had begun destroying crops because of low prices.

He said the reports were having a negative impact on an industry already suffering the lowest coffee prices in years and an unusally wide gap between Vietnamese export prices and those in London of $350-$400 per tonne.
Traders said rains had returned to Daklak last Friday after three days of dry weather, but played down the impact.
"Mould is not a serious issue at the moment. What you do see around is water-damaged beans," one said.
Current prices were quoted at a little over $1,000 per tonne FOB Saigon Port, in extremely quiet trade.
Nhan said Vietnam had exported some 40,000 tonnes of coffee from its 1996/97 crop so far and was expecting total output of at least 250,000 tonnes.
